rows.title: When Chinese manufacturing met Small Town, USA
rows.standfirst: Over the past decade, politicians from both parties have courted American voters with an enticing economic prospect – the dream of bringing manufacturing and manufacturing jobs back to America. They've pushed for that dream with tariffs and tax breaks and subsidies. But what happens when one multinational company actually responds to those incentives, and tries to set up shop in Small Town, USA?

rows.title: Why U.S. workers keep getting more productive
rows.standfirst: For the last couple of years, U.S. labor productivity has been on the rise. And economists don't know exactly why. So today on the show, the president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago plays economic detective and helps us investigate some different theories about why U.S. workers seem to be more productive than in prior decades.

rows.title: Hiring slowed in May, as employers added 139,000 jobs
rows.standfirst: U.S. employers added 139,000 jobs in May — a modest slowdown from the previous month. The unemployment rate held steady at 4.2%, as the workforce shrank.

rows.title: Sen. Tim Kaine says Trump's tariffs could reduce federal debt, but at what cost?
rows.standfirst: NPR's Steve Inskeep speaks with Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., who is also on the Senate Budget Committee, about how President Trump's tariffs will affect the federal budget and the economy.

rows.title: From 1,300 to 81 workers: Trump official plans to cut Voice of America to the bone
rows.standfirst: Trump senior advisor Kari Lake envisions the agency that includes the international broadcaster Voice of America with 81 staffers after mid-August — down from about 1,300 full-time employees and contractors.

rows.title: What the Trump-Musk breakup may mean for SpaceX and Tesla
rows.standfirst: From space travel to military operations to the future of green energy, the U.S. has become reliant on Elon Musk's business empire. But it won't be easy for the government to end its reliance on Musk.

rows.title: Why some economists are worried about U.S. inflation data
rows.standfirst: The federal government is scaling back data collection used to calculate the inflation rate because of staff shortages. Economists warn that could make for less accurate cost-of-living measures.

rows.title: Gilded Age 2.0?
rows.standfirst: To hear President Trump tell it, the late 1800s, i.e. the Gilded Age, were a period of unparalleled wealth and prosperity in the U.S. But this era was also marked by corruption and wealth inequality. Sound familiar? On today's show, is history repeating itself?

rows.title: Trump's tariffs could cut deficit by $2.8 trillion over next decade -- with caveats
rows.standfirst: The Congressional Budget Office projected President Trump's tariffs could raise trillions of dollars over the next decade — but they could also lead to higher inflation and slower economic growth.

rows.title: Partisan battle lines form over Trump's plan to defund NPR & PBS
rows.standfirst: Senate Democrats warn Trump plan to wipe out public broadcasting funding will shut down stations, eliminate essential services. But House GOP scheduled to vote to clawback $1.1 billion next week.

rows.title: Some federal workers lost health coverage they had paid for. A Democrat wants answers
rows.standfirst: Commerce Department employees who were fired, reinstated, and fired again learned belatedly that their health insurance has been cut off. Some had already racked up thousands in medical bills.

rows.title: Steel tariffs double. And, Congress asked to eliminate public broadcasting funds
rows.standfirst: Tariffs on imported steel and aluminum are doubling today. Here's how it could impact your wallets. And, Trump has asked Congress to wipe out funding for public broadcasting.

rows.title: With steel tariffs doubling today, a North Carolina manufacturer wonders how to compete
rows.standfirst: President Trump is doubling tariffs on steel and aluminum to 50%. It's designed to protect domestic steel and aluminum workers, but critics say it will raise prices for those that use the metals.

rows.title: An indicator lost: big disaster costs
rows.standfirst: The U.S. government has tallied the economic impact of major natural disasters going back to 1980. State and local governments used this data for budgeting and planning. But last month, the administration retired its Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters disaster database. Today on the show, we speak to Adam Smith, the architect of the program, on the work he did and what might be next.

rows.title: Trump's crypto interests (Two Indicators)
rows.standfirst: Today on the show – our crypto president. Just before President Donald Trump began his second administration in January, he and his business partners launched the $TRUMP coin. It's a memecoin that quickly raked in hundreds of millions of dollars. And there's a lot of earning potential still left on the table. Is that even legal?

rows.title: Why I joined DOGE
rows.standfirst: What was it like to work inside Elon Musk's DOGE? The cost-cutting initiative promised transparency, but most of its actions have been shrouded in secrecy.For months, there were reports of software engineers and Trump loyalists entering agencies and accessing sensitive data. DOGE also helped the Trump administration lay off thousands of government workers. NPR reporters have been trying for months to get anyone from DOGE to talk on the record. Now, Sahil Lavingia, a former DOGE staffer assigned to the Department of Veteran Affairs, is speaking. Today, what drew Sahil to DOGE and what he learned about the inner workings, in a way we've never heard before.For more on DOGE and the federal workforce: - The last time we shrank the federal workforce - Can... we still trust the monthly jobs report? - Can the Federal Reserve stay independent? This episode was hosted by Kenny Malone and Bobby Allyn. It was produced by Sam Yellowhorse Kesler and Emma Peaslee. It was edited by Jess Jiang and fact-checked by Sierra Juarez. rows.title: 'Buy now, pay later:' a replacement for the millennial lifestyle subsidy?
rows.standfirst: The cheap convenience of the "millennial lifestyle subsidy" has gone - does "buy now, pay later" fill in the gaps?

rows.title: Oil prices jump and stocks tumble following Israel's attack on Iran
rows.standfirst: Israel's attack on Iran sparked the biggest jump in crude oil prices since Russia's invasion of Ukraine more than three years ago. Stocks fell sharply.

rows.title: Trump's parade, FEMA phase out, and Warner Bros. Discovery divorces ... itself?
rows.standfirst: It's ... Indicators of the Week! Our weekly look at some of the most fascinating economic numbers from the news.

rows.title: Asian shares slide while oil prices surge after Israel's strike on Iran
rows.standfirst: Markets in Asia opened lower early Friday while oil prices surged after Israel attacked Iran's capital amid the ramping up tensions over Tehran's rapidly advancing nuclear program.

rows.title: What led the Boeing 787 Dreamliner to crash in India with 242 people aboard?
rows.standfirst: "It just appears to me that the airplane is unable to climb," former NTSB investigator Jeff Guzzetti tells NPR. Several explanations could account for that, the aviation expert says.

rows.title: Why there's an unexpected surge in people claiming Social Security
rows.standfirst: Some early filers say worries about the future under the Trump administration moved up their timelines.

rows.title: House votes to kill funding for public media
rows.standfirst: The U.S. House voted Thursday on a rescission bill to claw back money for foreign aid programs, along with the next two years of funding for the public media system. The measure now goes to the Senate.

rows.title: She served the American people for 35 years. Now her retirement income is on the line
rows.standfirst: As part of Trump's "Big, Beautiful Bill," the House voted to end a retirement supplement aimed at helping federal employees who retire before they're 62.

rows.title: The hidden costs of healthcare churn
rows.standfirst: Healthcare churn—when people switch insurance plans—is particularly bad in the US.

rows.title: Are Trump's tariffs legal?
rows.standfirst: When President Trump announced his sweeping new tariffs this year, many trade law experts were startled. Typically, presidents don't have the authority to impose broad tariffs with a snap of their fingers.

rows.title: Supreme Court press corps asks chief justice to live-stream court's opinions
rows.standfirst: The press corps' letter was sent to the chief justice a year ago, but there has been no response.

rows.title: Inflation is holding steady as Trump's tariffs have yet to fully hit
rows.standfirst: Consumer prices in May were up 2.4% from a year ago, but inflation eased on a monthly basis, according to the latest figures from the Labor Department

rows.title: Here's how climate change is affecting your home insurance
rows.standfirst: Insurance costs are soaring, and coverage is hard to find in some parts of the United States. Communities say insurers are ignoring their efforts to confront the problem.

rows.title: ABC drops Terry Moran after he calls Trump a 'world-class hater'
rows.standfirst: In dropping veteran correspondent Terry Moran, ABC News said his post calling President Trump "a world-class hater" was "a clear violation of ABC News policies."

rows.title: Reporters for Voice of America and other U.S. networks fear what's next
rows.standfirst: Journalists who have risked their freedom to report for Voice of America and its sister news outlets wonder what happens to them now that the Trump administration has gutted their parent agency.

rows.title: The U.S. is the world's bribery cop. Is that about to change?
rows.standfirst: The U.S. has been policing bribery all over the world for nearly half a century using a law called the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act. But now, President Trump has said that this anti-corruption law is crippling American businesses. Since taking office, his administration has reduced the number of investigators, killed some cases, and changed the rules.

rows.title: Kari Lake guts Voice of America as U.S. reporters face threats abroad
rows.standfirst: The Trump administration is slashing jobs at Voice of America's parent agency by 85%. Journalists who have risked their freedom to report for the broadcaster wonder what happens next.

rows.title: SALT-n-pessimism
rows.standfirst: It's ... Indicators of the Week! Our weekly look at some of the most fascinating economic numbers from the news.

rows.title: Deadly listeria outbreak leads to recall of ready-to-eat fettuccine Alfredo meals
rows.standfirst: A nationwide listeria outbreak has been linked to 17 illnesses, and three deaths, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Food Safety and Inspection.

rows.title: The debt limit, the origins of the X Date, and why it all matters
rows.standfirst: Note: A version of this episode first ran in 2023.

rows.title: Pro-Trump media figures split over the U.S. role in the Israel-Iran conflict
rows.standfirst: Many of President Trump's nominal media allies are breaking with him over his backing of Israel, arguing it will lead to a wider war.

rows.title: Trump pushes back TikTok's sell-by date for a third time
rows.standfirst: Last year, Congress banned the app in the U.S., citing national security concerns and demanding it spin off from its Chinese owner, ByteDance. Trump has again paused enforcement of the ban.

rows.title: Social Security benefits face big cuts in 2033, unless Congress acts
rows.standfirst: Trustees of the Social Security trust fund predict the fund will be exhausted in eight years. Unless Congress acts, Social Security payments will automatically drop by 23% at that time.

rows.title: 'Labubu' is a plush toy that is causing a frenzy. Here's its origin story
rows.standfirst: Labubus are a global sensation — sparking long lines outside toy stores, selling out online within minutes, and listing for double or triple their original price on resale markets. Here's why.

rows.title: Fed holds interest rates steady, signals rate cuts of 0.5% later this year
rows.standfirst: The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady Wednesday. Members of the central bank's rate-setting committee also telegraphed their plans for possible rate cuts later this year.

rows.title: Why the 30-year bond matters
rows.standfirst: Last week, the U.S. Treasury held an auction for 30-year bonds. Some were worried no one would show up to buy these things! That didn't happen, but the 'long bond' isn't exactly thriving at the moment. Today on the show, we look back at why we have such a long maturity bond and why it might be a good idea to start paying attention to it going forward.

rows.title: How Apple turbocharged China's development
rows.standfirst: A new book raises the specter that corporate offshoring of manufacturing may have undermined America's lead in technological innovation and even its national security.

rows.title: 10 ways travel insiders deal with annoying flight delays
rows.standfirst: Clever advice on how to quickly rebook your flight, skip long lines and avoid flight issues in the future. One tip? Try queuing up for an agent in the airport lounge.

rows.title: Mixing family business with US trade policy in Vietnam
rows.standfirst: Last month, Eric Trump, executive vice president at The Trump Organization, attended a ceremony in Vietnam to break ground on a $1.5 billion residential development and golf course. This comes as Vietnam's government is in trade talks with the administration of Eric's father, President Donald Trump.

rows.title: Senate considers ditching the EV tax credit even earlier than planned
rows.standfirst: As the Senate debates the giant tax and spending bill, lawmakers are weighing a Sept. 30 end date for the EV tax credits. The bill still needs to pass the Senate and then go through reconciliation.

rows.title: Judge OKs sale of 23andMe — and its trove of DNA data — to a nonprofit led by its founder
rows.standfirst: The DNA data of millions of people who used 23andMe's services won't be sold to a pharmaceutical company. A bankruptcy judge greenlighted the sale of the remnants of the firm, including its wealth of genetic data, to a nonprofit led by co-founder Anne Wojcicki.

rows.title: Canada ditches digital tax after tariff threat from Trump
rows.standfirst: Canada scrapped a digital services tax that would have hit U.S. tech companies such as Google and Amazon after President Trump halted trade talks and threatened higher tariffs on Canadian imports.

rows.title: This company wants to be the first to mine the ocean floor, with Trump's help
rows.standfirst: The Metals Company is applying for permission from the Trump administration to mine for nickel and cobalt beneath a remote patch of the Pacific Ocean. Other countries say the minerals aren't America's to mine.

rows.title: Can Starlink stay ahead in satellite internet?
rows.standfirst: Whether you're watching Love Island in an RV or streaming a playlist in a remote California campground, if you're using satellite internet, odds are you're using Elon Musk's Starlink.

rows.title: Canadian prime minister says U.S. trade talks resume after Canada rescinded tech tax
rows.standfirst: President Trump said Friday that he was suspending trade talks with Canada over its plans to continue with its tax on technology firms, which he called "a direct and blatant attack on our country."

rows.title: Here comes the bridal gown tariff
rows.standfirst: How much extra would you pay to see your dream come true? It's always a big question for wedding-planning couples. Now, there's a new twist courtesy of U.S. trade policy.

rows.title: 'Kisses yes, Bezos No,' protesters say, as Bezos wedding stirs controversy in Venice
rows.standfirst: Protesters denounced the three-day celebrations for the wedding between Jeff Bezos and his wife Lauren Sanchez Bezos as a symbol of rising inequality and disregard for the city's residents.

rows.title: J.M. Smucker plans to remove artificial colors from its jams and other products
rows.standfirst: Smucker joins a growing number of big food companies that have announced plans to eliminate artificial dyes.

rows.title: Opinion: Remembering Bill Moyers
rows.standfirst: NPR's Scott Simon remembers the astonishing career of former White House press secretary and long-time public broadcasting journalist Bill Moyers, who died this week at the age of 91.

rows.title: Less bang for your buck: Even the July 4 fireworks may be hit by tariffs this year
rows.standfirst: Fans of fireworks may face higher prices this Fourth of July. That's because most fireworks are made in China and importers now have to pay tariffs of at least 30%.

rows.title: When Trump met crypto
rows.standfirst: In 2019, President Trump tweeted: "I am not a fan of Bitcoin and other Cryptocurrencies." Today, the Trumps are all over crypto.

rows.title: Remembering war correspondent Rod Nordland
rows.standfirst: After surviving many close calls as a war correspondent, Norland was diagnosed with a lethal brain tumor in 2019. He died June 22. In this 2024 interview, he reflected on facing mortality.

rows.title: Stocks climb to new record highs
rows.standfirst: Both the S&P 500 index and the Nasdaq closed at record highs on Friday, as investors shrugged off trade tensions and recent fighting in the Middle East.

rows.title: Solar manufacturing is booming. Advocates say it could go bust without incentives
rows.standfirst: Abruptly ending tax incentives that encourage solar developers to buy American could upend a booming manufacturing sector.
